executor: BOOTSTRAP_EXECUTOR (Claude Code, outside AutoLoop lifecycle, per Controller authorization, continuing the Phase 0A/0B BOOTSTRAP_EXCEPTION)

Q1_canVerificationOnlyPhasesRemoveArbitr.detail: The reviewer role is this codebase's verification-only role by contract (sectionAuthority already declared "You have NO tools and NO mutation authority"). src/lifecycle-runner.mjs's callAdapter() now hard-pins toolPolicy: { mode: "no-tools" } for phase === "reviewer" unconditionally, independent of taskCard.toolPolicy. This maps to Pi's real --no-tools CLI flag (src/adapter/pi-rpc-adapter.mjs toolPolicyArgs), not a prompt string.

Q2_enforcementOrInstructionOnly.answer: HARD_TOOL_SURFACE for the reviewer role specifically; SOFT_POLICY still for the executor role.
Q2_enforcementOrInstructionOnly.detail: REVIEWER_TOOL_POLICY is applied at the adapter-request layer in lifecycle-runner.mjs, before the child Pi process is even spawned with args — it is a real CLI flag to Pi's own runtime (--no-tools), not persuasion. This is enforcement, not instruction, FOR THE REVIEWER ROLE. The executor role still needs real shell (it's the writer/test-runner role) and its toolPolicy is unchanged — its bounded-verification protection remains the Phase 0B soft policy (operative prompt instruction) plus the pre-existing harness-owned runVerificationCommand() path (src/v2/harness-evidence.mjs), which the lifecycle already uses as the authoritative verification command rather than trusting the model's own shell narration for evidence.
Q2_enforcementOrInstructionOnly.caveat: "Enforcement" here means AutoLoop's own adapter never grants the reviewer child process any tool access, and Pi's own CLI is trusted to honor --no-tools (this repo's own adapter comment already states Pi is not OS-sandboxed; a compromised or buggy Pi build could still in principle disregard its own flag — that residual trust boundary is unchanged and out of this bootstrap's scope).

Q3_boundedWallClockTimeout.detail: src/adapter/pi-rpc-adapter.mjs already implements a per-request timeoutMs with a real kill sequence: setTimeout fires an RPC abort first, then escalates to SIGTERM on the child's process group after graceMs, then SIGKILL after a second grace window if still alive (terminateChild()). This is exercised against a real spawned child process in test/test-pi-rpc-adapter.mjs T16 ("timeout without any abortSignal yields status=timed_out with process tree cleaned up", 200ms timeout) and T15/T15b (abort escalating through SIGTERM/SIGKILL with no orphan, including a descendant grandchild). None of this was added by VCA-1 — it pre-dates this card and was verified, not built, in this phase.
Q3_boundedWallClockTimeout.productionValueNotFoundInRepo: No committed call site in this repo sets timeoutMs for a real production run (only test fixtures, e.g. scripts/ta2-verify.mjs / ta2r-verify.mjs use timeoutMs: 90000 for scripted/test configs). The real production timeoutMs value — and therefore the actual wall-clock budget a real Pi verification phase gets — is caller-owned, set outside this repository. This bootstrap cannot prove what timeout, if any, was in effect during the original 896s incident.

Q4_canThe896sFailureModeStillExecute.answer: PARTIALLY_MITIGATED_NOT_ELIMINATED — see caveat below; this is not a clean YES/NO/ONLY_IF_SOFT_POLICY answer.
Q4_canThe896sFailureModeStillExecute.detail: For any run that goes through src/lifecycle-runner.mjs + src/adapter/pi-rpc-adapter.mjs (the only real Pi-invocation path found in this repo): (a) a reviewer-role phase can no longer receive shell tool access at all (Q1/Q2, hard), (b) an executor-role phase that DOES have shell access and runs a pathological unbounded command is still bounded by whatever timeoutMs the caller configured (Q3, hard mechanism, soft/unknown configured value), and (c) both roles' operative prompt now explicitly forbids constructing such a command and requires HOLD instead (Phase 0B, soft).
Q4_canThe896sFailureModeStillExecute.unresolvedGap: This bootstrap could not find, anywhere in this repository, the production glue code that (i) sets a real toolPolicy/timeoutMs for a live card run, or (ii) proves that the original 896s grep was issued from inside this adapter's spawned Pi child at all, as opposed to a separate interactive Pi session run directly by the Controller (following card instructions much like this very VCA-1 exchange) that never goes through src/adapter/pi-rpc-adapter.mjs. If the latter is what actually happened, none of Phase 0A/0B/0C's code changes touch that path — only the prompt-text and guard-module artifacts are available to it, and only if that separate session's own operative instructions are drawn from this repo's phase-response-contract.mjs text (unconfirmed).

changesImplemented.change: Added REVIEWER_TOOL_POLICY = { mode: "no-tools" } constant; callAdapter() now passes phase === "reviewer" ? REVIEWER_TOOL_POLICY : taskCard.toolPolicy instead of taskCard.toolPolicy unconditionally for both roles.
changesImplemented.gapClosed: Previously taskCard.toolPolicy (a single value from hooks.toolPolicy) was passed identically to both the executor and reviewer adapter requests. The reviewer's own prompt (sectionAuthority, phase-response-contract.mjs) has always claimed "You have NO tools", but nothing in the code enforced that independent of what toolPolicy the caller configured for the executor. A caller configuring a permissive executor toolPolicy (e.g. to let the writer run tests) was silently also granting that same tool access to the reviewer's Pi invocation.
changesImplemented.scopeCheck: This is a 3-line functional change (one constant, one ternary) plus explanatory comments — matches the "very small" Phase 0C mandate. No sandbox, no Colima migration, no new daemon, no Pi architecture change.

notImplemented_outOfScope: OS-level sandboxing of Pi's shell tool for the executor role (Pi's own docs already state it has no built-in sandbox; closing this fully is a sandboxing project, explicitly excluded by the Controller's Phase 0C scope fence)

Restricting executor toolPolicy to a denylist of discovery tools (grep/find) — executor legitimately needs general shell for writer/test work; narrowing it risks breaking real writer phases and was not requested
